title: Chapter 58: Management of the Poisoned Patient
source: Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, 16th Edition, Chapter 58 (Craig Smollin; Stephen Petrou)
file: Katzung Chapter 58_ Management of the Poisoned Patient.pdf
lecture: 10/13 (Toxic Responses) and 10/14 (Treating Poisonings); the treating-poisonings lecture continues 10/19
about: The chapter reviews the basic principles of poisoning, initial management, and specialized treatment of poisoning, including methods of increasing the elimination of drugs and toxins. It defines toxicokinetics and toxicodynamics and describes how volume of distribution, clearance, first-pass metabolism, protein binding and first-order versus zero-order elimination change in overdose, and how therapeutic index and the shape of the dose-response curve determine the severity of an intoxication. It describes how poisoned patients die, the ABCD supportive measures, the toxicologically oriented history and physical examination, laboratory and imaging procedures (anion gap, osmol gap, electrocardiogram) and the limits of toxicology screening. It then covers skin and gastrointestinal decontamination (gastric lavage, activated charcoal, cathartics and whole bowel irrigation), specific antidotes (Table 58-3) and methods of enhancing elimination (dialysis, urinary pH manipulation). A final section describes common toxic syndromes, from acetaminophen to theophylline, with the clinical features and treatment of each.

lecture_use.point: Drugs with a large volume of distribution leave the blood for tissue reservoirs, so they are hard to remove by hemodialysis; the deck's list of large-Vd (>5 L/kg) drugs (antidepressants, antipsychotics, antimalarials, opioids, propranolol, verapamil) is the chapter's list.

lecture_use.point: Hemodialysis must be prolonged because drug sequestered in tissues only slowly re-enters the blood where the extracorporeal method can reach it.
lecture_use.chapter_location: Special Aspects of Toxicokinetics - Volume of Distribution; Methods of Enhancing Elimination - A. Dialysis Procedures; Table 58-2 Hemodialysis in drug overdose and poisoning

lecture_evidence.quote: So these people that have overdosed on drugs with very large volumes of distribution, you probably are going to have to do hemodialysis for a long time to start getting the drug moving out of its sequestration site back into the blood, and then pulled off by your extracorporeal removal method, right?

lecture_use.point: Overdose saturates hepatic metabolism, reducing the first-pass effect so more drug reaches the circulation.

lecture_evidence.quote: OK, the third bullet point says clearance can can be messed up and overdosed because if you saturate liver metabolism, you get a reduced first pass effect and then more drug is in circulation.

lecture_use.point: Poisons may injure the gastrointestinal epithelial barrier and thereby increase absorption (her example: caustic iron destroying the saturable active-transport protection).

lecture_evidence.quote: I want to point out the second bullet here where we say drugs may injure the gastrointestinal tract, increasing absorption, OK?

lecture_use.point: At very high blood concentrations plasma protein-binding capacity is exceeded, raising the free fraction and the toxic effect.

lecture_evidence.quote: The next to bottom bullet, uh, when you've got overdose situation, you may exceed protein binding capacity.

lecture_use.point: Toxicodynamics: both the therapeutic index and the overlap of therapeutic and toxic response curves must be considered; the deck's Drug A / Drug B sedation-hypnosis-anesthesia-coma figure (credited to Katzung) is the graded dose-response figure the chapter cites.
lecture_use.chapter_location: Special Aspects of Toxicodynamics (page 2; refers to Figure 22-1)

lecture_evidence.quote: When we are thinking about drugs and overdose and wondering if their pharmacodynamics are changing in that massive dose, you need to think about the therapeutic index and the overlap between what's a therapeutic dose, what's the therapy look like, and then what's the toxic response to a dose. So this is illustrated by this graph on the right hand side. We've got drug A and drug B.

lecture_use.point: Drug A with a linear dose-response curve reaches coma while drug B with a plateauing curve does not, so two drugs that look alike at the therapeutic dose differ in overdose.

lecture_evidence.quote: But drug A, you keep increasing the dose, and you just happen to get a linear response with this, and you get a coma for drug A, even though with the dose, the same dose drug B, you only get almost anesthesia, OK?

lecture_use.point: Tricyclic antidepressant intoxication reduces sweating while increasing muscular activity or seizures, so heat cannot be dissipated (lethal hyperpyrexia).

lecture_evidence.quote: So, the TCAs, they reduce sweating. In an overdose situation, that's one of their pharmacodynamic effects. At the same time that they are increasing muscular activity and potential for seizures, OK?

lecture_use.point: Beta blocker and calcium channel blocker overdoses alter not only cardiac function but blood flow to the kidney and liver, slowing elimination of the toxin.

lecture_evidence.quote: Reducing blood flow to the kidneys and the liver, you're reducing the body's ability to eliminate the drug.

lecture_use.point: Gastric lavage: a large orogastric/nasogastric tube is placed, fluid is instilled and withdrawn; the chapter restricts it to awake patients or a protected airway.

lecture_evidence.quote: Also, activated charcoal, because of its chemistry, it's only going to grab a certain kinds of compounds that somebody might have ingested, right?

read_for: Special Aspects of Toxicokinetics - Volume of Distribution: why a large Vd (>5 L/kg) defeats hemodialysis, and the lists of large-Vd drugs (antidepressants, antipsychotics, antimalarials, opioids, propranolol, verapamil) and small-Vd drugs (<1 L/kg: salicylate, acetaminophen, ethanol, phenobarbital, lithium, valproic acid, phenytoin).

Special Aspects of Toxicokinetics - Clearance: the paragraph listing how overdose alters kinetics (slowed dissolution or gastric emptying, GI epithelial injury increasing absorption, reduced first-pass effect, exceeded protein-binding capacity, first-order elimination becoming zero-order with a prolonged half-life) - every deck bullet on that slide comes from it.

Special Aspects of Toxicodynamics: therapeutic index versus overlap of therapeutic and toxic curves, drug A (linear) versus drug B (plateau), the tricyclic sweating/seizure hyperpyrexia example and the beta blocker/calcium channel blocker effect on renal and hepatic elimination.

Decontamination - B. Gastrointestinal Tract: emesis no longer recommended; gastric lavage technique and airway requirement; activated charcoal 10:1 ratio and the poisons it does not bind; repeated-dose charcoal 'gut dialysis'; whole bowel irrigation with GoLYTELY/CoLyte at 1-2 L/h until the rectal effluent is clear.
Table 58-2 Hemodialysis in drug overdose and poisoning: the drugs for which hemodialysis may be indicated and those for which it is not useful (the Vd principle in practice).
Methods of Enhancing Elimination of Toxins - A. Dialysis Procedures: why efficiency depends on molecular weight, water solubility, protein binding, endogenous clearance and distribution.

Beta Blockers and Calcium Channel Blockers sections: the two classes whose evidence-based out-of-hospital guideline abstracts she assigned (glucagon for beta blockers; whole bowel irrigation and charcoal for sustained-release calcium antagonists, calcium, high-dose insulin).
Case Study and Case Study Answer: activated charcoal slurry by nasogastric tube as the example of preventing absorption.

terms.chapter_definition: the absorption, distribution, excretion, and metabolism of toxins, toxic doses of therapeutic agents, and their metabolites.
the injurious effects of these substances on body functions.

the apparent volume into which a substance is distributed in the body; a mathematical representation that describes, inversely, how much of the drug remains in the vascular system. A large Vd implies the drug distributes from the blood to other tissues and is not readily accessible to measures aimed at purifying the blood, such as hemodialysis.
a measure of the volume of plasma that is cleared of drug per unit time; the total clearance for most drugs is the sum of clearances via excretion by the kidneys and metabolism by the liver.
If the capacity of the liver to metabolize a drug is exceeded, the first-pass effect will be reduced and more drug will be delivered to the circulation.
At normal dosage, most drugs are eliminated at a rate proportional to the plasma concentration.

If the plasma concentration is very high and normal metabolism is saturated, the rate of elimination may become fixed; this change may markedly prolong the apparent serum half-life and increase toxicity.

Both the therapeutic index and the overlap of therapeutic and toxic response curves must be considered; two drugs may have the same therapeutic index but unequal safe dosing ranges if the slopes of their dose-response curves are not the same.
removing toxins from the skin or gastrointestinal tract, undertaken simultaneously with initial stabilization, diagnostic assessment, and laboratory evaluation.

performed, if the patient is awake or the airway is protected by an endotracheal tube, using an orogastric or nasogastric tube as large as possible; lavage solutions (usually 0.9% saline) should be at body temperature.

owing to its large surface area, can adsorb many drugs and poisons; most effective if given in a ratio of at least 10:1 of charcoal to estimated dose of toxin by weight; does not bind iron, lithium, or potassium, and binds alcohols and cyanide only poorly.

repeated doses of oral activated charcoal may enhance systemic elimination of some drugs (including carbamazepine, dapsone, and phenobarbital) by a mechanism referred to as 'gut dialysis', although the clinical benefit is unproved.

a balanced polyethylene glycol-electrolyte solution (GoLYTELY, CoLyte) given orally at 1-2 L/h (500 mL/h in children) for several hours until the rectal effluent is clear; enhances gut decontamination after ingestion of iron tablets, enteric-coated medicines, illicit drug-filled packets, and foreign bodies.

more efficient than peritoneal dialysis; its efficiency is a function of the molecular weight, water solubility, protein binding, endogenous clearance, and distribution in the body of the specific toxin.

listen:
This reading is Chapter 58, Management of the Poisoned Patient, from Katzung's Basic and Clinical Pharmacology, sixteenth edition. It belongs to the Toxic Responses lecture of October thirteenth and the Treating Poisonings lecture of October fourteenth, which continues on October nineteenth. The card marks the chapter as not discussed in class as a reading, and readings are tested as discussed. But her October fourteenth lecture drew these points from it.

First, toxicokinetics. Drugs with a large volume of distribution leave the blood for tissue reservoirs, so they are hard to remove by hemodialysis. The chapter's list of large volume drugs is antidepressants, antipsychotics, antimalarials, opioids, propranolol and verapamil. She said, "overdose drugs with large volumes of distribution, they're hard to remove from the, they're hard to remove from the blood, OK?" Hemodialysis must run a long time to pull drug back out of tissue. Second, clearance in overdose. She said, "if you saturate liver metabolism, you get a reduced first pass effect and then more drug is in circulation." Poisons may injure the gastrointestinal tract and increase absorption, and protein binding may be exceeded. Third, toxicodynamics. She said, "you need to think about the therapeutic index and the overlap between what's a therapeutic dose, what's the therapy look like, and then what's the toxic response to a dose." Drug A with a linear curve reaches coma while drug B with a plateau does not. She asked, "Which one can you increase the dose and not have an unwanted adverse effect? B." Tricyclic antidepressants reduce sweating while increasing muscular activity and seizures. Beta blocker and calcium channel blocker overdoses reduce blood flow to the kidney and liver, slowing elimination. Fourth, decontamination. Emesis is no longer recommended. She said, "What's the risk of emesis? Aspiration is the biggest risk." Gastric lavage is pumping the stomach with a tube. Whole bowel irrigation uses a polyethylene glycol electrolyte solution such as GoLYTELY. Activated charcoal grabs only certain compounds, and the chapter says it does not bind iron, lithium or potassium. Multiple dose charcoal is used when the substance undergoes enterohepatic recirculation.

On what is testable: on October fourteenth she said, "Every example I give you is testable because it explains the concept that we're going to deal with, OK?" The specific antidotes in Table 58 dash 3 and the common toxic syndromes were not reached and are deferred to October nineteenth.

Re-read first Special Aspects of Toxicokinetics and Toxicodynamics, then the Gastrointestinal Tract decontamination section.
